title: Fossil-fuel-free electric propulsion for large, long-range passenger aircraft

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a large passenger aircraft that uses electric propulsion to carry a useful passenger payload over long routes without consuming fossil fuel. Success requires the complete aircraft to perform a useful transport mission: its energy supply, electrical equipment, propulsion, cooling and safety systems must work together within acceptable mass and operating limits. NASA’s electrified-aircraft work supports this integrated-system framing, but the supplied evidence does not demonstrate the full capability.

Conceptual scope: batteries, fuel cells or another energy architecture could potentially supply the electric propulsion system. These alternatives would require separate aircraft-level evaluations. Electric motors alone do not establish fossil-fuel-free operation, because electricity can also come from an onboard fossil-fuel-burning generator. Conversely, using a nonfossil fuel in a conventional combustion engine would address a different propulsion concept. The defining outcome here combines electric propulsion, fossil-fuel-free energy and useful large-aircraft long-range performance.

significance.text: If achieved in practical passenger service, this capability could change the energy supply of long-range aviation and reduce its dependence on liquid fossil fuels. NASA identifies reduced fossil-fuel use as a rationale for aircraft electrification. Extending that objective to a large aircraft completing an entire long-range mission without fossil fuel would represent a substantially broader capability than reducing fuel use through hybrid assistance.

Conditional consequences: a deployable system could shift some aviation energy demand toward electricity production or nonfossil energy carriers, with corresponding changes to airport energy infrastructure and aircraft servicing. The scale of that shift would depend on payload, route coverage, fleet adoption, energy availability and operating economics. A successful demonstrator would establish technical capability within its tested mission; it would not by itself establish widespread replacement of conventional aircraft.

Climate and economic implications remain conditional. Fossil-fuel-free operation does not automatically establish low lifecycle emissions: energy production, fuel or battery manufacture, infrastructure and replacement requirements would need evaluation. Non-CO₂ flight effects would also require assessment for the chosen architecture. The supplied sources do not quantify these effects or establish net climate improvement or commercial competitiveness. Comparisons with electric road transport are limited by aircraft weight, power and cooling constraints; a better battery or electrification of selected flight phases alone would not establish this innovation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is an integrated energy and electric-propulsion system that provides both enough usable energy for a long mission and enough power for the aircraft’s operating demands, while preserving useful passenger payload. These are different requirements: power describes the rate of energy delivery, while energy determines how long it can be sustained. NASA states that large electrified aircraft require megawatt-level power and identifies weight, cooling, component development, aircraft integration and certification as challenges. Meeting a power rating alone does not establish long-range endurance.

Engineering synthesis: the relevant mass accounting must include the installed system, rather than only an energy-storage material or individual component. Depending on the architecture, that accounting would encompass storage, containment, electrical conversion and distribution, propulsion equipment, cooling and protective systems. Batteries would require assessment of usable stored energy and power under flight conditions; fuel-cell approaches would additionally require assessment of fuel storage and conversion equipment. Infrastructure, reliability and safe operation are further evaluation areas. The supplied NASA material supports several integration challenges, but does not establish a complete barrier analysis for every possible architecture.

The earlier 1,000 Wh/kg figure is not validated here as an aircraft-level threshold for long-haul flight. The supplied record does not establish its original derivation, whether it refers to cells or an installed system, or which payload, route, reserve and aircraft assumptions it uses. It should therefore remain an unresolved numerical assertion rather than a completion requirement. The evidence neither validates that number nor proves that no useful numerical threshold has been developed elsewhere.

current_state.text: In an article dated July 20, 2026, NASA reported flight of a Saab 340B fitted with a megawatt-class hybrid-electric engine developed through work with GE Aerospace. The reported engine integrated electric motors, a gas turbine and energy storage. This is a relevant aircraft-level integration demonstration. Its hybrid architecture and reported fuel-saving operation, however, do not demonstrate a large passenger aircraft completing a long-range mission without fossil fuel.

NASA’s Electrified Aircraft Propulsion FAQ independently states that large electrified aircraft require megawatt-level power. It distinguishes small all-electric aircraft from larger hybrid configurations and discusses weight, cooling, component development and eventual certification. The copy described in the supplied review carried a December 31, 2025 update date. Its earlier testing plans should be read in that temporal context; they do not contradict the subsequent July 2026 flight report. Neither source supplies a validated 1,000 Wh/kg long-haul requirement.

Evidence coverage is limited to the supplied research and review. The review describes complete, untruncated copies of both relevant NASA pages, and the source index records no extraction issues for them. Nevertheless, the supplied search record is empty, and the material does not establish comprehensive coverage through the review’s November 1, 2026 reference date. The July demonstration can be reported at its stated date, but cannot be identified from this record as the latest development. Likewise, the full target capability is not demonstrated by these sources; that evidentiary limit is not proof that no other relevant achievement exists. Coverage is predominantly U.S. institutional material, with weaker coverage of commercial, non-English and classified work.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a transport-category aircraft should carry a representative passenger payload over a commercially meaningful long-range route using electric propulsion and no fossil fuel, while meeting the reserves applicable to the defined mission. Before evaluation, specify passenger payload, route distance, flight conditions, reserve requirements and what counts as fossil-fuel-free operation across all relevant onboard systems. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not published NASA completion requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Fossil-fuel-free electric propulsion carries long-range passenger missions with required reserves

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification: independently document installed-system mass, usable energy, power delivery and mission energy accounting, including auxiliary loads and thermal-management demands. Evidence should establish that the payload and range were achieved together in the reported configuration. Repeated missions and turnaround cycles should test whether performance is reproducible, with disclosure of charging or refueling conditions, maintenance, component replacement and any operational restrictions.
completion_criteria.label: Independent full-system accounting verifies reproducible payload and range together

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: demonstrate a credible certification path and assess lifecycle emissions using explicit energy-production, manufacturing, infrastructure and replacement boundaries. NASA’s discussion makes aircraft integration and certification relevant, but does not prescribe these exact tests. Repeated flights over a defined operating envelope would establish demonstrated breadth, not capability on every long-range route or under every condition. Claims of commercial competitiveness would require further operational evidence on cost, reliability, utilization, infrastructure and energy supply.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate credible certification path and assess lifecycle emissions within explicit boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison with AER-09, Sustained, useful air-breathing hypersonic flight: both concepts require a complete aircraft to deliver useful mission performance, so an isolated propulsion-component result is insufficient for either. Their central objectives differ. AER-09 concerns sustained useful hypersonic flight; AER-10 concerns fossil-fuel-free electric passenger transport over long routes. Neither capability establishes the other.

Roster comparison with AER-01, Mass-access orbital transportation: both would require operationally useful vehicles, credible safety and repeatable service. Their missions and completion evidence remain distinct. An electric passenger aircraft would not establish economical orbital access, and a reusable orbital vehicle would not establish fossil-fuel-free long-range passenger flight.

Roster comparison with AER-05, Economically competitive space-to-Earth solar power: electricity supplied by such a system could hypothetically contribute to aviation’s upstream energy supply. That is an optional downstream connection, not a prerequisite for AER-10. Competitive electricity delivery from space would not solve aircraft storage, mass, power or certification requirements, while AER-10 could draw on other nonfossil energy sources.

At the level of the supplied roster, AER-02’s interstellar probe, AER-03’s extraterrestrial propellant production, AER-04’s deep-space life support, AER-06’s robotic space construction, AER-07’s asteroid defense and AER-08’s life-search observatory are separate capabilities. Broad engineering overlap in energy, thermal control or reliability does not make any of them a completion criterion for this aircraft concept. No merger or dependency among these entries is established by the supplied evidence.

change_log.reason: The useful innovation is large, long-range fossil-fuel-free electric passenger transport; a component specification alone does not define or demonstrate it.

change_log.reason: The review supports the former directly but does not establish an exhaustive barrier analysis for batteries, fuel cells or every alternative architecture.

change_log.change: Retained the 1,000 Wh/kg issue as an unresolved numerical assertion and removed any implication that it is a validated threshold or definitively disproven.
change_log.reason: Its derivation, measurement boundary and mission assumptions were not supplied; lack of validation here does not resolve its validity elsewhere.

change_log.change: Preserved the July 20, 2026 Saab 340B demonstration, its megawatt-class scale and its motor, gas-turbine and energy-storage architecture.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports the dated flight report while distinguishing hybrid integration from the proposed fossil-fuel-free long-range capability.

change_log.change: Added the FAQ’s December 31, 2025 update context and qualified claims about the latest state of the field.
change_log.reason: Earlier testing plans do not contradict a subsequent flight, and the empty supplied search record cannot establish comprehensive coverage through November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Expanded significance to distinguish fossil-fuel displacement from lifecycle climate benefits, deployment scale and commercial competitiveness.
change_log.reason: Those downstream outcomes require additional evidence and do not follow automatically from electric propulsion.

change_log.change: Made completion criteria explicitly proposed and added advance specification of mission conditions, independent installed-system accounting, repeated operations and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These additions make the concept assessable without presenting editorial proposals as established standards or finite testing as universal proof.

change_log.change: Added explicit roster comparisons and preserved the source-access and coverage limitations relevant to AER-10.
change_log.reason: Related outcomes remain distinct, and complete extraction of two NASA pages does not establish comprehensive knowledge of the field.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether the full target capability remained unmet as of November 1, 2026, or whether later relevant demonstrations occurred.
Large aircraft, representative passenger payload, long range, required reserves and repeatable turnaround still need quantitative operational definitions before completion can be evaluated.
The origin and validity of the 1,000 Wh/kg figure remain unresolved, including whether it describes cells, packs or an installed aircraft system.
No architecture-specific mass, energy, storage, thermal, safety or infrastructure analysis is supplied that establishes feasibility for the full mission.
Lifecycle climate effects, including non-CO₂ effects for the chosen architecture, and commercial competitiveness remain unquantified.
The evidence base remains concentrated in two NASA sources and does not establish broad coverage of commercial, non-English or classified developments.

brief.title: Long-range electric airliners without fossil fuel
possible: Passengers could travel long distances in large planes driven by electric motors, without the aircraft consuming fossil fuel. The plane would carry a useful passenger load and enough spare energy to meet flight safety requirements.
why: Airlines could reduce their dependence on liquid fossil fuels for long-distance travel. Airports would need ways to supply electricity or other nonfossil energy sources and service the aircraft that use them.

sources.who: NASA, GE Aerospace, BETA Technologies and Boeing
sources.showed: A passenger aircraft flew with a system combining electric motors, a fuel-burning engine and energy storage. This demonstrated that these parts could work together in flight.
sources.quote: Mounted to a Saab 340B aircraft, the engine flew at Farnborough International Air Show in the United Kingdom.
sources.cited_for: It supports the case that electric motors and an aircraft’s other power equipment can work together in flight.
sources.not_established: The flight did not demonstrate a large passenger aircraft completing a long route without fossil fuel.

sources.showed: NASA explains why weight and heat constrain electric aircraft. Its overview describes small battery-powered planes and larger planes that combine electric motors with fuel-burning engines.
sources.quote: In current power systems, 20% of energy is dissipated as excess heat that must be cooled.
sources.cited_for: It explains why the weight and cooling needs of the whole aircraft matter.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate an energy system light enough to carry passengers over long routes without fossil fuel.

shown: NASA and GE Aerospace have demonstrated flight with electric motors working alongside a fuel-burning engine. Their system powered a modified passenger aircraft, but it still combined electricity with combustion.
missing: A large electric passenger plane has yet to demonstrate a useful long-distance mission without fossil fuel, including required spare energy.
The complete energy system must supply enough energy for the journey and deliver it fast enough, while leaving room and weight for passengers.
Independent measurements and repeated flights must establish that passenger load and range hold up together through normal servicing cycles.
A credible route to safety approval and an assessment of emissions across the aircraft’s working life remain necessary.

milestones.label: A full passenger mission without fossil fuel
milestones.explanation: A large passenger aircraft would have to complete a defined long route using electric motors and no fossil fuel, with required spare energy. This would demonstrate the complete transport mission.

milestones.label: Independent checks confirm repeatable passenger load and range
milestones.explanation: Independent checks would have to account for all installed equipment, weight, energy use and power delivery across repeated flights and servicing cycles. This would confirm that passenger load and range are achieved together.

milestones.label: A credible safety approval path and lifetime emissions assessment
milestones.explanation: The aircraft would need a credible path to safety approval and an emissions assessment covering energy supply, manufacturing, infrastructure and replacements. These would establish practical safety and environmental boundaries.

uncertain: The required aircraft size, passenger load, distance, spare energy and time between flights still need clear definitions.
Avoiding fossil fuel during flight does not establish a net climate benefit; effects beyond carbon emissions also depend on the chosen energy system.
Whether these aircraft could compete on cost, reliability and frequency of use remains unknown.

page.title: Long-range all-electric passenger aircraft
page.definition: An airliner carries at least 200 passengers nonstop for at least 5,000 nautical miles (9,260 km) without consuming fossil fuel on board. Electric motors provide all thrust, drawing power from batteries, hydrogen fuel cells, or both. A fuel cell converts hydrogen and oxygen into electricity. At regional scale, Heart Aerospace has reported a 27-minute battery-electric flight of its X1 demonstrator.

goal.need: In 2023, flights departing from EU27 and EFTA airports emitted 133 million tonnes of CO₂. Flights over 4,000 km accounted for 6% of departures and 46% of those emissions. More efficient jets burn less kerosene, but each kilogram they burn still releases about 3.16 kg of CO₂. Passengers could cross an ocean without the aircraft burning fossil fuel. The net emissions saving depends on how the electricity for charging or the hydrogen for fuel cells is produced.

figures.caption: Long-haul shares of EU27+EFTA departures and their CO₂ emissions in 2023
figures.note: Long-haul means flights longer than 4,000 km. The inventory covers flights departing from EU27 and EFTA airports.

statements.quote: right through to 200+ seats with a 5,000nm range
statements.context: Written evidence to the Scottish Affairs Committee describes the company’s hydrogen-electric powertrain roadmap.
Think Paper 21 assessed a hypothetical Paris–Singapore widebody using the battery energy density available in 2023.

completion.title: A certified electric airliner carries 200 passengers for 5,000 nautical miles without fossil fuel.
completion.criterion: A type-certified airliner completes a nonstop commercial flight carrying at least 200 passengers for at least 5,000 nautical miles (9,260 km). Electric motors provide all propulsive power and receive all their electricity from onboard batteries, hydrogen fuel cells, or both. No onboard system consumes fossil fuel. The flight complies with approved operating limitations and the competent authority’s applicable fuel or energy planning, alternate and final-reserve requirements.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational criterion. ZeroAvia specifies the hydrogen-electric seat capacity and range. No outside body identified specifies the combined loaded-flight test for either energy system.
completion.basis: ZeroAvia’s roadmap gives seats and range. The Atlas requires the stated passenger load and distance on the same commercial flight and applies the test to both energy systems. The responsible authority governs design approval and operating requirements.

milestones.title: Electric-airliner propulsion components pass laboratory validation at technology readiness level 4.
milestones.criterion: A propulsion component or its bench model performs its intended basic function in the laboratory. Documented measurements agree with the predicted performance, and the conditions relevant to its intended aircraft use are identified.
milestones.set_by: ATI FlyZero, Technology Roadmaps, Figure 6, and NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 4.

milestones.title: An electric-airliner propulsion prototype operates in a relevant environment at readiness level 6.
milestones.criterion: A representative model or prototype of the electric propulsion subsystem operates under the environmental conditions critical to its intended aircraft application. It addresses the critical effects of scale, and documented measurements agree with predicted performance.
milestones.set_by: ATI FlyZero, Technology Roadmaps, Figure 6, and NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 6.
milestones.threshold_quote: Subsystem model or prototype demonstration in relevant environment

milestones.title: An electric-airliner system prototype is demonstrated in flight at technology readiness level 7.
milestones.criterion: An aircraft flies with a representative prototype of the electric propulsion system operating in its intended airborne environment. The prototype addresses the critical effects of scale for the application claimed, and its measured in-flight performance agrees with predictions.
milestones.set_by: ATI FlyZero, Technology Roadmaps, Figure 6, and NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 7.

milestones.title: A 200-passenger, 5,000-nautical-mile electric airliner receives aircraft type-design approval.
milestones.criterion: The responsible aviation authority issues a type certificate or approves a change to the type design of the airliner designed to carry at least 200 passengers for at least 5,000 nautical miles. The approval covers the installed electric propulsion and energy systems. The applicant demonstrates compliance of the aircraft, including its structure, engines, controls, electrical systems and flight performance, with the applicable certification basis.
milestones.set_by: EASA, Aircraft certification. This is the regulator’s general aircraft approval test; the passenger capacity and range define the Atlas entry’s subject.
milestones.threshold_quote: If technically satisfied with the compliance demonstration by the applicant, EASA closes the investigation and issues the certificate.

milestones.title: A laboratory experiment validates a predicted electric-propulsion function at readiness level 3.
milestones.criterion: For a critical function or characteristic of the proposed electric propulsion technology, analysis predicts a measurable parameter and a laboratory experiment validates that prediction. The analytical and experimental results are documented.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 3.
milestones.threshold_quote: Analytical and experimental proof-of-concept of critical function and/or characteristics.

milestones.title: An electric-propulsion component passes tests in a relevant environment at readiness level 5.
milestones.criterion: A component or representative physical model operates with realistic supporting equipment under conditions relevant to its critical functions on the aircraft. Test measurements agree with predictions, and the requirements for scaling the component to its intended application are documented.
milestones.set_by: ATI FlyZero, Technology Roadmaps, Figure 6, and NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 5.

milestones.title: The target airliner’s electric propulsion system qualifies for flight at readiness level 8.
milestones.criterion: Testing and analysis demonstrate the completed propulsion system in its final configuration for the intended airliner and its operating environment. Documented tests verify performance predictions, and any life testing necessary for that system is complete.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 8.
milestones.threshold_quote: Actual system completed and "flight qualified" through test and demonstration.

not_found: No published acceptance protocol was found for ZeroAvia’s 200+ seat, 5,000-nautical-mile goal.
No flight or aircraft type certificate meeting the combined passenger, range and onboard energy criterion was found for either energy system.
No final-reserve energy duration specific to a 200-passenger all-electric airliner was found.

results.finding: The X-57 Mod II’s four 55 kW cruise motor controllers passed functional and dynamometer tests.
results.detail: The 55 kW figure is the stated maximum output per controller. The report does not give the measured output or the predicted value for the dynamometer runs.
results.quote:
Each controller completed individual printed 
circuit board/hardware checkouts, functional tests on an unloaded 
motor, high-power acceptance and proto-qualification tests on a 
dynamometer test stand, and vibration and thermal testing.

results.finding: Ground runs on one X-57 with 72 kW-class cruise motors established the vibration profile used to qualify its controllers.
results.detail: The tailored profile used lower vibration energy than the standard general aviation test and added margin above the measured ground vibration.
results.quote:
The 
units were declared flight worthy after passing all tests.

results.finding: One X-57 Mod II ground-test aircraft ran its installed electric propulsion subsystem for vibration measurements.
results.detail: The ground runs captured installation-specific vibration. The report identifies possible differences between ground and flight vibration.
results.quote:
Armstrong researchers measured the electric motor vibration 
environment during ground motor runs of the X-57 aircraft 
configuration dubbed Modification II (Mod II).

results.finding: One Wright Electric motor exhibited zero partial-discharge events in a laboratory altitude simulation.
results.detail: The motor insulation result applies to both energy-system cases because the test concerns voltage and ambient pressure at the motor. The announcement leaves the power source unspecified.
results.quote: The system exhibited zero partial discharge events at all test conditions, indicating that Wright’s innovative insulation system is performing as designed.

results.finding: One Wright Electric motor exhibited zero partial-discharge events in a laboratory altitude simulation.
results.detail: The motor insulation result applies to both energy-system cases because the test concerns voltage and ambient pressure at the motor. The announcement leaves the power source unspecified.
results.quote: The system exhibited zero partial discharge events at all test conditions, indicating that Wright’s innovative insulation system is performing as designed.

results.finding: Airbus demonstrated one 1.2 MW hydrogen propulsion system.
results.quote: In 2023, Airbus successfully demonstrated a 1.2MW hydrogen-propulsion system

results.finding: Airbus completed end-to-end testing of one integrated fuel-cell propulsion assembly in 2024.
results.detail: Airbus planned further ground testing with the propulsion bench and hydrogen distribution system for 2027.
results.quote: in 2024, end-to-end testing of an integrated fuel cell stack, electric motors, gearboxes, inverters and heat exchangers was completed.

results.finding: BALIS fuel-cell string model validation against bench data gave 3.3% mean absolute percentage error at steady low power. Run count unspecified.
results.detail: The authors attributed the high-power voltage overshoot to an air-supply response lag omitted from the model. Validation of the liquid-hydrogen tank model was pending.
results.quote:
A good agreement between the simulation and experimental data was observed 
for low power levels and stationary conditions wi th an MAPE of 3.3  %.

results.finding: The two-motor BALIS e-drive reached its specified 600 kW peak electrical input in single-mode bench testing. Run count unspecified.
results.detail: The bench campaign also identified torque oscillations and recorded a motor defect that the authors attributed to possible contamination in the cooling loop.
results.quote:
Maximum peak electrical power of 600 kW at 17,000 rpm 
for ten minutes and continuous electrical power of 500 kW were achieved in single-mode operation according to the 
specifications of the manufacturer.

results.finding: One 10-module BALIS fuel-cell assembly produced 1,020 kW in a partly parallel ground test.
results.detail: Separate facility buses emulated the effect of DC–DC converters. The liquid-hydrogen supply was modeled separately and remained pending integration into the test facility.
results.quote:
A power output of 1020 kW and with that the MW proof 
of performance of the UUT was achieved.

results.finding: One magni650 electric propulsion unit delivered 700 kW under simulated flight conditions.
results.detail: The release does not specify the testbed’s electrical supply or supporting equipment.
results.quote: The magni650 successfully performed at an altitude of 30,000 feet at a maximum continuous power of 700 kilowatts (kw) – an unprecedented achievement for an electric engine.

results.finding: One magni650 electric propulsion unit operated at a simulated altitude of 30,000 feet.
results.detail: The planned Dash 7 demonstration would replace one of four turbine engines with a magni650 powertrain. The reported result comes from the ground testbed.
results.quote: The magni650 successfully performed at an altitude of 30,000 feet at a maximum continuous power of 700 kilowatts (kw) – an unprecedented achievement for an electric engine.

results.finding: ZA600 fuel-cell modules delivered 170 kW each at simulated takeoff in one ground test.
results.detail: The test reproduced aircraft power demand. The release does not specify which aircraft environmental conditions the test facility reproduced.
results.quote: During the 2 hour and 38 minute test, the fuel cell system demonstrated stable power output and excellent performance of the balance-of-plants, with each 200kW capable module producing 170kW power for take-off, 132kW during a 23-minute climb and 83kW for a 90-minute cruise.

results.finding: One certification-intent ZA600 fuel-cell power generation system completed a simulated 250-nautical-mile flight profile on the ground.
results.detail: The ZA600 application described is for aircraft with up to 20 seats. Full engine ground testing of the final design was still planned.
results.quote: The test simulated a 250 nautical mile flight in a Cessna Caravan 208b aircraft, equivalent to flying between London Heathrow and Dublin Airport.

results.finding: Heart Aerospace’s battery-electric X1 demonstrator delivered more than 1 MW of propulsion power on its first piloted flight (n=1).
results.detail: The FAA experimental airworthiness certificate covered a test profile that included taxi, takeoff, climb, maneuvering, and landing.
results.quote: The piloted mission lasted 27 minutes, during which X1 reached an altitude of 1,100 feet AGL and its all-electric propulsion system delivered more than one megawatt of power.

results.finding: H2FLY’s HY4 liquid-hydrogen fuel-cell demonstrator completed four piloted test flights, with the longest lasting more than three hours.
results.detail: The 1,500 km figure is an estimate of maximum range based on the flight tests. The release reports flight duration and gives no distance flown.
results.quote: The H2FLY team has completed four flights powered by liquid hydrogen as part of its flight test campaign, including one flight that lasted for over three hours.

results.finding: One Joby hydrogen fuel-cell electric air taxi demonstrator completed a 523-mile flight.
results.detail: The test used a converted Joby air taxi prototype with a liquid-hydrogen tank and reduced battery mass.
results.quote: On June 24, 2024, Joby’s hydrogen-electric technology demonstrator aircraft completed a 523-mile flight above Marina, California, with no in-flight emissions except water.

results.finding: One Joby pre-production battery-electric air taxi prototype completed more than 25,000 miles of testing before conversion.
results.detail: Joby gives a cumulative test distance without a flight count or individual flight results.
results.quote: The converted aircraft previously completed more than 25,000 miles of testing as a battery-electric aircraft at Joby’s base in Marina, CA.

results.finding: China’s civil aviation authority issued a type certificate for one aircraft type, the four-seat battery-electric RX4E.
results.detail: The developer’s university news article reports the certification decision. The supplied text does not include the regulator’s certificate or decision record.

results.finding: Two full-scale X-57 high-lift propellers ran stably in wind-tunnel tests with 439 averaged data points. Left-hand torque agreed closely with predictions.
results.detail: Load-cell cross-loading and thermal drift limited thrust validation. The right-hand propeller produced less torque than predicted across most test points.
results.quote:
Both propellers 
demonstrated very stable operation throughout the test including during deployment, stowing, 
and windmilling.

results.finding: Hydrogen PEM fuel-cell system, 480-point parameter study: optimized controls increased maximum net power by 29% at low pressure.
results.detail: The 480 points were used to fit the models. The 29% gain compares optimized and default control settings and does not quantify agreement between predicted and measured net power.
results.quote:
At 497 hPa, the net power increase is as high as 29%, see 
the red line with the corresponding axis on the right in Figure 1a.

results.finding: One WM2500 prototype motor was tested at a simulated altitude of 40,000 ft.
results.detail: The altitude test reports full voltage. The source gives no measured thrust or shaft power at altitude and no comparison with predictions.
results.quote: The motor was tested to full voltage of 800V at a simulated altitude of 40,000 feet.

results.finding: In flight tests of one battery-electric e-Genius prototype, cooling drag accounted for 6% of zero-lift drag.
results.detail: The excerpt reports broad agreement with preliminary predictions and gives no numerical measure of that agreement.
results.quote:
Als Vorgri auf Kapitel 5.2.1 sei an dieser Stelle erwähnt, dass der
Kühlwiderstand im Flugversuch einen Anteil von 6 % zum Nullwiderstand beigetragen
hat.

results.finding: The Rapid 200-FC hydrogen fuel-cell system generally matched model predictions in two 40-minute flight tests.
results.detail: Both missions presented for validation were included in the six-flight parameter fit. The comparison therefore establishes agreement on data used for fitting.
results.quote:
These comparisons were carried out over
two ﬂight tests, and an excellent agreement was
observed between the modelled and experimental
data in the thermal management subsystem behav-
iour, which describes the temperature dynamics in
the FCS.

definition = "An airliner carries at least 200 passengers nonstop for at least 5,000 nautical miles (9,260 km) without consuming fossil fuel on board. Electric motors provide all thrust, drawing power from batteries, hydrogen fuel cells, or both. A fuel cell converts hydrogen and oxygen into electricity. At regional scale, Heart Aerospace has reported a 27-minute battery-electric flight of its X1 demonstrator.". Reason: The definition should make clear that the passengers and range belong to one nonstop flight and distinguish the target from a regional-scale flight demonstration.

goal.need = "In 2023, flights departing from EU27 and EFTA airports emitted 133 million tonnes of CO\u2082. Flights over 4,000 km accounted for 6% of departures and 46% of those emissions. More efficient jets burn less kerosene, but each kilogram they burn still releases about 3.16 kg of CO\u2082. Passengers could cross an ocean without the aircraft burning fossil fuel. The net emissions saving depends on how the electricity for charging or the hydrogen for fuel cells is produced.". Reason: The emissions figures establish the size of the problem, but the final sentence omits what passengers would gain and how the energy supply affects that benefit.
add statement by EUROCONTROL, 2023: "too heavy to take off". Reason: EUROCONTROL’s widebody study supplies a missing assessment of the feasibility of the battery-electric case.

edit completion: criterion = "A type-certified airliner completes a nonstop commercial flight carrying at least 200 passengers for at least 5,000 nautical miles (9,260 km). Electric motors provide all propulsive power and receive all their electricity from onboard batteries, hydrogen fuel cells, or both. No onboard system consumes fossil fuel. The flight complies with approved operating limitations and the competent authority\u2019s applicable fuel or energy planning, alternate and final-reserve requirements."; set_by = "Atlas operational criterion. ZeroAvia specifies the hydrogen-electric seat capacity and range. No outside body identified specifies the combined loaded-flight test for either energy system."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; threshold_quote = "200+ seats with a 5,000nm range"; threshold_ref = 3; basis = "ZeroAvia\u2019s roadmap gives seats and range. The Atlas requires the stated passenger load and distance on the same commercial flight and applies the test to both energy systems. The responsible authority governs design approval and operating requirements."; refs = [3, 2, 5, 7]. Reason: The current wording would admit a turbine burning non-fossil fuel to generate electricity for the motors, outside both defined energy systems.

add milestone after None: "A laboratory experiment validates a predicted electric-propulsion function at readiness level 3.". Reason: The sequence starts at component validation and skips the earlier laboratory proof of a critical function at readiness level 3.

edit m1: criterion = "A propulsion component or its bench model performs its intended basic function in the laboratory. Documented measurements agree with the predicted performance, and the conditions relevant to its intended aircraft use are identified."; set_by = "ATI FlyZero, Technology Roadmaps, Figure 6, and NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 4."; threshold_quote = "Component validation in laboratory environment"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 24]. Reason: The level 4 criterion mixes the laboratory test with project results and omits the source’s threshold wording.

add milestone after m1: "An electric-propulsion component passes tests in a relevant environment at readiness level 5.". Reason: The roadmap distinguishes testing a component under relevant operating conditions from demonstrating an integrated subsystem.

edit m2: criterion = "A representative model or prototype of the electric propulsion subsystem operates under the environmental conditions critical to its intended aircraft application. It addresses the critical effects of scale, and documented measurements agree with predicted performance."; set_by = "ATI FlyZero, Technology Roadmaps, Figure 6, and NASA, NPR 7123.1D, Appendix E, hardware readiness level 6."; threshold_quote = "Subsystem model or prototype demonstration in relevant environment"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 24]. Reason: The level 6 criterion lists individual ground tests without specifying how the subsystem demonstration addresses scale and the intended operating environment.

edit m3: criterion = "An aircraft flies with a representative prototype of the electric propulsion system operating in its intended airborne environment. add milestone after m3: "The target airliner’s electric propulsion system qualifies for flight at readiness level 8.". Reason: The sequence jumps from flight of a prototype to aircraft type approval and omits qualification of the propulsion system in its final configuration.
